Q168461.name: Bordeaux
facts: Its 1855 classification ranked the great châteaux of the Left Bank, from first growth to fifth.
The Gironde estuary splits it into a gravelly Left Bank and a clay-rich Right Bank.
Its red blends are often called claret in Britain, a trade dating back to the Middle Ages.

Q1016093.name: Burgundy
facts: Its vineyards are cut into hundreds of tiny named plots, the climats, now a World Heritage Site.
Romanée-Conti, among the world's most expensive wines, grows on less than two hectares here.
Cistercian monks mapped its slopes plot by plot in the Middle Ages.

Q134862.name: Champagne
facts: Only sparkling wine made here, fermented a second time in the bottle, may carry its name.
Miles of chalk cellars run under the towns of Reims and Épernay.
Dom Pérignon, a Benedictine monk, worked at the abbey of Hautvillers here.

Q80114014.name: Alsace
facts: Unusually for the country, its wines are labelled by grape and sold in tall, slim flute bottles.
The Vosges mountains shelter it from rain, making it one of the country's driest corners.
It changed hands with its eastern neighbour four times between 1871 and 1945.

Q1954580.name: Loire Valley
facts: Its vineyards follow the country's longest river for hundreds of kilometres, past royal châteaux.
Vouvray, Chinon and Pouilly-Fumé all lie along it.
Its whites run from bone-dry to honeyed, often from Chenin Blanc.

Q1891041.name: Rhône Valley
facts: Côte-Rôtie and Hermitage cling to steep granite slopes in its northern half.
Its southern half is swept by the mistral, a cold dry wind from the north.
Its northern reds are made from Syrah alone; the south blends Grenache with up to a dozen others.

Q616.name: Beaujolais
facts: Every third Thursday of November, its 'nouveau' is released weeks after the harvest.
Nearly all its red wine comes from the Gamay grape.
Ten crus, among them Fleurie, Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent, sit on its granite hills.

Q1058259.name: Chablis
facts: Its vineyards sit on Kimmeridgian clay, packed with fossil oyster shells.
It lies so far north that spring frosts are fought with heaters and sprinklers among the vines.
Its crisp whites are made from Chardonnay, usually with little or no oak.

Q282221.name: Sancerre
facts: A hilltop town looks over its vineyards of flinty, chalky soil.
Its whites made Sauvignon Blanc famous long before New Zealand did.
Pouilly-Fumé faces it across a river.

Q1805438.name: Languedoc-Roussillon
facts: One of the largest wine regions in the world, stretching along the Mediterranean to the Pyrenees.
Blanquette de Limoux, from here, claims to be older than Champagne.
Much of the country's bulk wine once came from its plains; today it is known for value reds.

Q815934.name: Provence
facts: Close to nine in ten of its bottles are pale, dry rosé.
Its oldest vineyards go back to Greek settlers who founded Marseille around 600 BC.
Bandol, on its coast, makes long-lived reds from Mourvèdre.

Q1713793.name: Jura
facts: Its 'vin jaune' ages for over six years under a film of yeast, unlike any other table wine.
Vin jaune comes in a squat 62 cl bottle, the clavelin.
Louis Pasteur grew up in Arbois, its wine capital, and studied fermentation there.

Q1435049.name: Médoc
facts: Château Lafite, Latour and Margaux all stand on its gravel banks.
It is a peninsula between the Atlantic and the Gironde estuary.
Pauillac and Saint-Julien, two of its villages, hold most of the 1855 first growths.

Q2715616.name: Saint-Émilion
facts: A medieval village here has a church carved into the limestone rock.
Its classification is revised about every ten years, unlike the fixed one across the river.
Château Cheval Blanc and Château Ausone are its most famous estates.

Q2914687.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
facts: The Avignon popes built a summer castle here in the 14th century.
Up to thirteen grape varieties may go into its wines.
Its vineyards are covered in large round stones, galets, that store the day's heat.

Q771636.name: Sauternes
facts: Autumn mists from the Ciron river bring on noble rot, which shrivels the grapes.
Château d'Yquem, the only 'superior first growth' of 1855, is here.
Pickers go through its vineyards several times, taking only the rotted berries.

Q1025792.name: Cahors
facts: Its inky red was known in medieval London as 'black wine'.
It is the old home of Malbec, long before Argentina made the grape famous.
Its vineyards line loops of the Lot river.

Q1954034.name: Muscadet
facts: Its dry whites come from Melon de Bourgogne, near the Atlantic coast.
Many are aged 'sur lie', resting on their spent yeast until bottling.
It is the classic match for oysters from the nearby coast, around Nantes.

Q750979.name: Chianti
facts: Its wines once came in a straw-covered flask, the fiasco.
A black rooster on the neck marks its Classico wines.
Its hills lie between Florence and Siena.

Q808584.name: Barolo
facts: Called 'the king of wines and the wine of kings', it must age at least 38 months.
Its wines are made from Nebbiolo, a grape named for the autumn fog of the Langhe hills.
In the 1980s and 90s its young modernists, with small new oak barrels, fought the traditionalists.

Q590461.name: Barbaresco
facts: A village of the Langhe hills, just across Alba from its more famous neighbour.
Angelo Gaja put its wines on the world map in the 1960s and 70s.
Its Nebbiolo reds need less ageing than their neighbour's - 26 months at least.

Q26667.name: Brunello di Montalcino
facts: Its wines come only from Sangiovese and age at least five years before release.
The Biondi-Santi family created the wine in the 19th century.
A hilltop fortress town above the Val d'Orcia gives it its name.

Q541959.name: Vino Nobile di Montepulciano
facts: Its 'noble wine' was praised by a 17th-century poet as the king of all wines.
Its Renaissance hill town is not to be confused with a grape of the same name grown further east.
Locally, its Sangiovese is called Prugnolo Gentile.

Q1069954.name: Prosecco
facts: It is made fizzy in large steel tanks, not in the bottle.
The steep hills of Conegliano and Valdobbiadene, where its best grows, are a World Heritage Site.
It outsells Champagne around the world, and is the base of an Aperol spritz.

Q852467.name: Valpolicella
facts: Amarone is made here from grapes dried on racks for months before pressing.
Its hills rise just north of Verona.
Ripasso is made by passing young wine over the leftover skins of Amarone.

Q1933708.name: Soave
facts: A walled medieval town with a castle sits in the middle of its vineyards.
Its white is made from Garganega, grown on old volcanic soils.
It was once the best-selling white of its country in the United States.

Q3750896.name: Franciacorta
facts: Its sparkling wine is made the same way as Champagne, bottle-fermented.
Its vineyards lie at the south end of Lake Iseo.
It is close to Brescia and an hour from Milan.

Q842052.name: Marsala
facts: An English merchant, John Woodhouse, began fortifying its wine in 1773 to survive the sea voyage.
Nelson's fleet carried it as a ration.
A port city on the western tip of an island gives the wine its name.

Q1146204.name: Lambrusco
facts: Its red wine is fizzy, often served chilled.
It comes from the plains around Modena, home of balsamic vinegar.
It is the name of both the wine and a family of grapes.

Q891340.name: Bolgheri
facts: A cypress-lined avenue five kilometres long leads to its village.
Sassicaia, a Cabernet Sauvignon that broke the local wine rules, was first made here in the 1940s.
Its vineyards lie on the Tyrrhenian coast, far from the classic hill towns of the region.

Q3733809.name: Etna
facts: Its vines grow on the slopes of Europe's most active volcano.
Some of its vineyards climb above 1,000 metres, among the highest in Europe.
Many of its vines were never grafted, as phylloxera could not live in its volcanic sand.

Q1946117.name: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo
facts: It is named after a grape, not after the Tuscan town that shares the name.
Its vineyards run from the Apennines down to the Adriatic coast.
Cerasuolo, its deep cherry-coloured rosé, comes from the same grape.

Q1569384.name: Rioja
facts: Its wines are labelled crianza, reserva or gran reserva by how long they aged.
Haro, one of its towns, holds a wine battle every June, where crowds soak each other in red.
It was the country's first wine to reach the top quality grade, DOCa, in 1991.

Q2167338.name: Ribera del Duero
facts: Vega Sicilia, one of the country's most famous estates, is here.
Its vineyards sit on a high plateau, around 800 metres up, with very hot days and cold nights.
Its reds are made from Tempranillo, known locally as Tinto Fino.

Q1754563.name: Priorat
facts: Its vines grow on llicorella, a crumbly slate that glitters in the sun.
Carthusian monks founded a priory here in the 12th century that gave it its name.
In the 1990s a small group of winemakers turned a forgotten region into a cult one.

Q16398.name: Jerez
facts: Its fortified wines age in a solera, where young wine tops up older barrels year after year.
Fino matures under a layer of yeast called flor that keeps air away from it.
Its vineyards grow on white albariza soil, which soaks up winter rain.

Q1433176.name: Rías Baixas
facts: Its name means 'lower inlets', after the fjord-like estuaries of the Atlantic coast.
Its vines are often trained high on granite posts, to keep the grapes away from damp.
Its whites come from Albariño and go with the local seafood.

Q356128.name: Rueda
facts: Its white wine comes from Verdejo, a grape it brought back from near-extinction.
It is famous for its whites, though it sits next door to a great red region.
Many of its vineyards are picked at night to keep the grapes cool.

Q2841161.name: Penedès
facts: Most of the country's sparkling Cava comes from here.
Its capital Vilafranca hosts castells, towers of people.
Its vineyards lie inland of Barcelona.

Q765567.name: Toro
facts: Napoleon's troops are said to have taken its wine with them.
Its reds, from a local strain of Tempranillo, are among the most powerful in Europe.
Its sandy soils kept its old vines safe from phylloxera.

Q6463671.name: La Mancha
facts: It is one of the largest single wine appellations in the world.
Don Quixote fought its windmills in Cervantes' novel.
Airén, the white grape that covers its plateau, was once the world's most planted.

Q624640.name: Bierzo
facts: Pilgrims on the Way of St James walk through its valleys.
Its reds come from Mencía, grown on steep slate slopes.
The Romans mined gold here at Las Médulas.

Q140379672.name: Douro Valley
facts: Its fortified wine was once carried downriver in flat-bottomed rabelo boats.
Its terraced vineyards on schist slopes became the world's first demarcated wine region, in 1756.
Port is aged in lodges across the river from the city of Porto.

Q1067753.name: Vinho Verde
facts: Its name means 'green wine', meaning young, not the colour.
Its whites are light, low in alcohol and often slightly fizzy.
Vines were once trained up trees and on pergolas here so crops could grow beneath.

Q27697.name: Madeira
facts: Its fortified wine is heated as it ages, a process called estufagem.
It was used to toast the US Declaration of Independence in 1776.
The wine comes from an Atlantic island far closer to Morocco than to its own mainland.

Q2832668.name: Alentejo
facts: About half of the world's cork comes from its forests of cork oak.
Some of its wineries still ferment in large clay pots called talhas, as the Romans did.
It covers roughly a third of its country, mostly hot rolling plains.

Q1269612.name: Dão
facts: Its vineyards sit on granite, ringed by mountains that keep out Atlantic rain.
Touriga Nacional, the country's great red grape, may have started here.
Its name comes from a river, a tributary of the Mondego.

Q672776.name: Mosel
facts: Some of its vineyards are among the world's steepest, with slopes of over 65 degrees.
Its Rieslings are grown on blue and red slate along a looping river.
Bernkastel's Doctor vineyard is said to have cured an archbishop.

Q387316.name: Rheingau
facts: Late harvest Riesling was discovered here in 1775 when the courier with permission to pick arrived late.
Schloss Johannisberg, one of the oldest Riesling estates, overlooks it.
Its vineyards face south, where the Rhine turns west for a while.

Q185439.name: Pfalz
facts: The world's oldest signposted wine route, opened in 1935, runs through it.
It is the second-largest wine region of its country, with a mild climate where figs grow.
The world's largest wine barrel stands in Bad Dürkheim.

Q567327.name: Rheinhessen
facts: It is the largest wine region of its country.
Liebfraumilch was first made here, around a church in Worms.
It lies inside a bend of the Rhine, between Mainz, Worms and Bingen.

Q153250.name: Franconia
facts: Its wines are bottled in the Bocksbeutel, a flat, round flask.
Its leading grape is Silvaner, not Riesling.
Würzburg's palace has huge wine cellars below it.

Q647902.name: Baden
facts: It is the warmest and southernmost wine region of its country.
Kaiserstuhl, an extinct volcano in it, is one of the sunniest spots in the land.
Its vineyards run 400 km from Lake Constance to near Heidelberg.

Q402640.name: Ahr
facts: Despite being one of the country's northernmost wine regions, it is mainly red.
A flash flood in July 2021 destroyed many of its wineries.
Its steep valley lies just south of Bonn.

Q192201.name: Wachau
facts: Its stone-walled vineyard terraces line the Danube, a World Heritage Site.
Its wines are graded Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd, after a grass, a falcon and a lizard.
Richard the Lionheart was held captive at Dürnstein castle here.

Q688060.name: Lavaux
facts: Its terraced vineyards rise steeply from the shore of Lake Geneva.
Cistercian monks built its terraces in the 12th century.
Its growers speak of three suns: the sky, the lake, and the stone walls.

Q828125.name: Tokaj
facts: Its sweet wine was praised as 'the wine of kings, the king of wines' by Louis XIV.
Sweetness of its Aszú wines was measured in puttonyos, baskets of rotten grapes.
It is one of the world's oldest classified wine regions, mapped from 1730.

Q987950.name: Eger
facts: Its red blend is called Bull's Blood, after legend of defenders who drank it in a 1552 siege.
The Valley of the Beautiful Women is lined with wine cellars cut into soft rock.
Its fortress held off a huge Ottoman army in 1552.

Q2223717.name: Santorini
facts: Its vines are woven into low baskets on the ground to protect the grapes from the wind.
Its vineyards grow on volcanic ash from a huge Bronze Age eruption.
Its whites come from Assyrtiko; its sweet Vinsanto from sun-dried grapes.

Q169674.name: Kakheti
facts: Wine has been made in this land for around 8,000 years, among the oldest on record.
Its winemakers ferment wine in qvevri, clay jars buried in the ground.
Its red wine is made from Saperavi, one of few grapes with red flesh.

Q202322.name: Beqaa Valley
facts: Château Ksara, its oldest winery, was founded by Jesuits in 1857.
It is a high valley between two mountain ranges, with Baalbek's Roman temples at its north end.
Château Musar kept making wine through its country's long civil war.

Q1115080.name: Commandaria
facts: It is the oldest named wine still made, called after the Knights' commandery.
It is made from sun-dried grapes grown on the southern slopes of the Troodos mountains.
Richard the Lionheart is said to have served it at his wedding.

Q1109872.name: Goriška Brda
facts: Its hills carry on across the border, where they are called Collio.
Its villages are known for cherries as well as orange wine.
Its winemakers revived ageing white wine on its skins, making it amber-coloured.

Q7038741.name: Ningxia
facts: Its vineyards stretch along the foot of the Helan Mountains.
The Yellow River runs through it, near the Great Wall.
Its winters are so cold that the vines are buried in soil every autumn.

Q1151105.name: Napa Valley
facts: At the 1976 Judgment of Paris, its wines beat the best of the old world in a blind tasting.
Robert Mondavi opened its first major winery since Prohibition in 1966.
A wine train runs along its valley from the town at its southern end.

Q7562180.name: Sonoma County
facts: It has more than a dozen sub-regions, among them the Russian River Valley.
Jack London's ranch was in its Valley of the Moon.
Morning fogs from the Pacific keep its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay cool.

Q2055633.name: Paso Robles
facts: It lies halfway between Los Angeles and San Francisco.
Its warm days and cold nights suit Zinfandel and Rhône grapes.
Tablas Creek brought Rhône vine cuttings here from Châteauneuf-du-Pape.

Q1867760.name: Lodi
facts: It is known as the Zinfandel capital of the world, with vines over a century old.
Its vineyards lie in the Central Valley, south of Sacramento.
It grows more wine grapes than Napa and Sonoma combined.

Q2223286.name: Santa Ynez Valley
facts: Much of the film 'Sideways' was shot here.
Its valleys run east to west, letting sea fog flow in from the Pacific.
Danish settlers founded the town of Solvang here.

Q919057.name: Willamette Valley
facts: Its Pinot Noir finished near the top of a 1979 blind tasting in Paris.
Burgundy's Drouhin family set up a winery here in 1987.
Its valley lies between the Coast Range and the Cascades, south of Portland.

Q7962694.name: Walla Walla Valley
facts: Its name is said to mean 'many waters' in the language of the local Sahaptin peoples.
Its vineyards cross a state line.
Sweet onions from here are almost as famous as its wine.

Q5450198.name: Finger Lakes
facts: Its long, narrow lakes were carved by glaciers.
Dr Konstantin Frank showed in the 1950s that European vines could survive its cold winters.
Its deep lakes keep the vineyards from freezing in winter.

Q634633.name: Texas Hill Country
facts: It is the second-most visited wine region in its country, after Napa.
German settlers founded Fredericksburg here in 1846.
Its warm limestone hills suit grapes from Spain and the Rhône.

Q1147919.name: Niagara Peninsula
facts: It is one of the world's largest producers of ice wine, from grapes frozen on the vine.
A long escarpment and a great lake keep its vineyards mild.
Its vineyards lie close to a famous waterfall on the border.

Q7081806.name: Okanagan Valley
facts: Its south end is desert, the only one in its country.
Its long, deep lake is said to hide a monster called Ogopogo.
Its vineyards sit at about 50 degrees north.

Q834310.name: Valle de Guadalupe
facts: It makes most of its country's wine.
Its vineyards lie inland from Ensenada, on the Pacific coast.
Russian Molokans, a religious group, settled it in the early 1900s.

Q721450.name: Maipo Valley
facts: It surrounds the capital, at the foot of the Andes.
Concha y Toro, one of the world's biggest wine companies, began here.
Its Cabernet Sauvignon is the country's most famous.

Q201304.name: Colchagua Valley
facts: Carmenère, once thought lost in Bordeaux, was rediscovered growing here in 1994.
Its vineyards follow the Tinguiririca river toward the Pacific.
Santa Cruz, its main town, has a wine train and a vintage festival.

Q3742.name: Casablanca Valley
facts: Its cool Pacific breezes made it the country's first great white wine region.
It lies on the road between the capital and the port of Valparaíso.
It was nearly all pasture until the 1980s.

Q166014.name: Mendoza
facts: Nearly three-quarters of its country's wine comes from here.
Its vineyards are watered by irrigation channels first dug by the Huarpe people.
Aconcagua, the highest mountain outside Asia, looks down on it.

Q7876801.name: Uco Valley
facts: Its vineyards climb past 1,500 metres up the Andes.
It lies south of the city that shares its province's name.
Its high altitude gives Malbec deep colour and freshness.

Q1025501.name: Cafayate
facts: Its vineyards lie among the highest in the world, around 1,700 metres up.
It is known for Torrontés, an aromatic white grape.
The red rock gorge of the Quebrada de las Conchas leads to it.

Q177231.name: Serra Gaúcha
facts: Italian immigrants from the Veneto planted its first vines in the 1870s.
Bento Gonçalves is its wine capital.
It is best known for its sparkling wines.

Q16577.name: Canelones
facts: Its vineyards lie just north of Montevideo.
Most of its country's wine is made here.
Tannat, brought by Basque settlers, is the country's signature grape.

Q5460.name: Stellenbosch
facts: It is the country's second-oldest European settlement, founded in 1679.
Its university town is known as the City of Oaks.
Its vineyards sit beneath the Simonsberg and Helderberg mountains.

Q1127722.name: Constantia
facts: Its sweet wine was sent to Napoleon in exile on St Helena.
Its oldest estate, founded in 1685 by the Cape's Dutch governor, is the country's oldest wine farm.
Its vineyards lie on the slopes of Table Mountain.

Q7653942.name: Swartland
facts: Its name means 'black land', after a dark bush that grows on its hills.
Its old, dry-farmed Chenin Blanc vines drove a winemaking revolution in the 2000s.
Its wheat fields and vineyards lie north of Cape Town.

Q4863063.name: Barossa Valley
facts: German-speaking Lutherans from Silesia settled it in the 1840s.
Some of its Shiraz vines are among the oldest in the world, planted in the 1840s.
Penfolds and Yalumba have made wine here for over 150 years.

Q6802082.name: McLaren Vale
facts: Its vineyards run down to the beaches of Gulf St Vincent.
The d'Arenberg Cube, a winery built like a Rubik's cube, stands here.
It lies just south of Adelaide.

Q1129760.name: Coonawarra
facts: It is famous for terra rossa, a strip of red soil over limestone, 15 km long.
Its Cabernet Sauvignon is among the country's best.
John Riddoch founded its first vineyards in 1890.

Q1612687.name: Clare Valley
facts: It is known for its dry Riesling, lean and limey.
Its growers led the switch from cork to screw caps in 2000.
The Riesling Trail, a cycling path, runs through its valley.

Q5944605.name: Hunter Valley
facts: It is one of the oldest wine regions in its country, planted in the 1820s.
Its Sémillon is picked early and ages for decades.
It lies north of Sydney, in coal mining country.

Q6759841.name: Margaret River
facts: Its first vineyards were planted in the late 1960s, after a scientist compared its climate to Bordeaux's.
It sits on a cape between two oceans, known for its surf.
Its Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay are among the country's most prized.

Q8049508.name: Yarra Valley
facts: It was the first wine region in its state to be planted, in 1838.
Moët & Chandon set up a winery here in 1986, Domaine Chandon.
It lies just northeast of Melbourne.

Q7687543.name: Tasmania
facts: Its wines come from an island south of the mainland, with a cool maritime climate.
Its sparkling wines are among its country's finest.
Its main vineyards follow the Tamar River near Launceston.

Q85783963.name: Marlborough
facts: Its Sauvignon Blanc made its country famous for wine in the 1980s.
Cloudy Bay, one of its wineries, is named after a bay Captain Cook named in 1770.
It sits at the northeast corner of an island, around Blenheim.

Q5061573.name: Central Otago
facts: It is the world's southernmost wine region.
Its vineyards lie in the mountains around Queenstown and Lake Wānaka.
Gold miners were the first to plant vines here, in the 1860s.

Q85765961.name: Hawke's Bay
facts: The Gimblett Gravels, an old riverbed, make some of its best reds.
Napier, an Art Deco city rebuilt after a 1931 earthquake, is in it.
It is the oldest wine region of its country, with vines from 1851.

Q1905554.name: Martinborough
facts: It is a small town in the Wairarapa, laid out in the shape of the Union Jack.
Its Pinot Noir is grown on old river terraces.
It lies over the hills from the capital.
